subtype: Reading a partner's or roommate's unspoken needs [Interpreting]
passage: I'm the third person in our flat, so I watch Arnab and Ramesh more than they realise. This week Ramesh changed. Dishes piled up on his side of the sink, his door stayed half-shut, and on Wednesday he snapped at Arnab over the Wi-Fi password, which he never does. I assumed he was angry with us. Arnab seemed to read it differently. He didn't lecture about the dishes. On Thursday night he knocked, leaned in the doorway and said, "You've seemed worn out. Do you want company or quiet?" I couldn't see Ramesh's face from the kitchen. There was a long pause, then: "Quiet. But maybe chai later?" Arnab said, "Deal," and closed the door gently. An hour later they were both on the balcony with two cups. I still don't know what was going on with Ramesh. Arnab might not know either. But he asked instead of guessing, and it seemed to help.

qa.q: What did Ramesh snap at Arnab about?
qa.a: The Wi-Fi password.

qa.q: What might Ramesh's piled-up dishes and half-shut door suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He may have been exhausted or overwhelmed and needing space, though the same signs could mean anger or plain busyness; when asked, he chose quiet first, then chai.

qa.q: Why was Arnab's question wiser than acting on a guess?
qa.a: It offered both options, company or quiet, so Ramesh could say what he needed instead of Arnab assuming.

qa.q: How did the narrator read Ramesh's mood at first?
qa.a: The narrator assumed Ramesh was angry with the flatmates, a reading Arnab chose not to act on.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult noticing a roommate's quietness, irritability and clutter, and checking whether they want company or quiet instead of assuming.

passage: In the cramped office of the college magazine in Kolkata, Neelam waited until the others had left for lunch before pulling up a chair beside Ojas. That morning, in the team meeting, his layout had been late again, and Soumya had said loudly, "Some of us actually meet deadlines." Ojas had gone red and not spoken for the rest of the meeting. Neelam didn't want to repeat that. "Can I give you some feedback on the layouts?" she asked. Ojas shrugged, arms crossed. "The last two issues reached the printer a day after the deadline. On Monday they charged us extra for the rush." She paused. "Your designs are the best part of the magazine. What if we set your deadline two days earlier and I check in on Wednesday?" Ojas uncrossed his arms. "The real problem is I get the final photos late. Can the photo team send them by Tuesday?" Neelam wrote it down. "Yes. Let's fix that first."

qa.q: When did Neelam talk to Ojas?
qa.a: After the others had left for lunch.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel after Soumya's comment in the meeting?
qa.a: Ojas felt humiliated and hurt, going red and silent, and was still defensive later, arms crossed.

qa.q: What made Neelam's feedback more useful than Soumya's?
qa.a: It was private, specific about the two late issues and the rush charge, included honest praise and a suggestion, and invited his side, which uncovered the late photos.

qa.q: What would have changed if Neelam had rebuked Ojas in the meeting too?
qa.a: Ojas would likely have grown more defensive and silent, and the real cause, the late photos, might never have come out.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult giving a team member private, timely feedback with specific examples and a suggestion, in contrast to a public rebuke.

subtype: Taking criticism without shrinking or bristling [Regulating]
passage:
In the small meeting room at the research centre, Nilesh tapped the printout.
"I've read your internship report. Honestly? The analysis is weak, and the whole thing reads like you rushed it."
Gurpreet breathed out slowly. "Okay. Can you show me where the analysis falls short?"
"Page six. You list the survey numbers but never say what they mean for the shop owners."
"That's fair. I can add a paragraph on that. What made it feel rushed?"
"The typos, mainly. And the formatting."
"The typos, yes, I'll fix them. But the fieldwork took three weeks. Is it the writing that feels rushed, or the research?"
Nilesh paused. "The writing. The fieldwork's actually solid."
"Thanks, that helps. So: what the numbers on page six mean, and a proper proofread. Anything else?"
"No. Send it on Friday."
That evening Gurpreet's sister phoned to ask how it went. "My first instinct was to argue, or to feel useless," Gurpreet said. "I did neither. I asked questions."

qa.q: On which page did Nilesh find the analysis weak?
qa.a: Page six.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet tempted to feel when the criticism came?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt the pull to argue defensively or to feel useless, but steadied with a slow breath.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet separate the useful points from the unfair one?
qa.a: By asking clarifying questions: accepting the page-six point and the typos, and asking whether "rushed" meant the writing or the research, which showed the fieldwork was solid.

qa.q: How did Nilesh's view shift during the talk?
qa.a: Nilesh moved from calling the whole report rushed to admitting the fieldwork was solid and only the writing needed work.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult taking criticism by listening, asking clarifying questions and separating useful points from unfair ones, without bristling or self-blame.

subtype: Contempt and ridicule as warning signs [Interpreting]
passage: You're the first person I'm saying this to properly, Sudha, so bear with me. I'm Kiran, and you know Tushar and I have been together a year. It wasn't one big thing. It was the eye-rolls whenever I talked about my dance classes. The little sneer, "Oh, here's the artist," in front of his friends. Last month I got a question wrong at trivia night and he did this slow clap, and everyone laughed. I laughed too. Then I went to the washroom and couldn't stop shaking. I used to tell myself it was just his humour. But jokes don't leave you feeling small every single time. On Saturday I said calmly, "When you mock my classes or roll your eyes at me, I feel disrespected. I need it to stop." He rolled his eyes again. So on Monday I went to the college counsellor, who helped me think it through. I'm not trading insults with him. I'm deciding what I deserve.

qa.q: What did Tushar do at trivia night?
qa.a: A slow clap after Kiran got a question wrong.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel after the trivia-night slow clap?
qa.a: Kiran felt humiliated and shaken, laughing along in public but unable to stop shaking in the washroom afterwards.

qa.q: What steps did Kiran take instead of trading insults?
qa.a: Kiran named the pattern calmly and set a clear limit, then went to the college counsellor when the eye-rolling continued.

qa.q: How might Tushar's friends have seen the sneers?
qa.a: Probably as harmless jokes, since they laughed, without seeing how small the mockery made Kiran feel.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult recognising sneering, mockery and eye-rolls in a relationship as warning signs, naming the pattern calmly, setting a limit and seeking help.

passage:
Wednesday, 11 p.m.
Two ultimatums in one day. Writing them down so I can think.
Morning: Mohan, my flatmate, said, "If you smoke on the balcony again, I'll have to move out. The smoke gets into my room and I can't breathe properly." Annoying, but fair. It's about his health, and he's leaving me a clear choice. I'll stop.
Evening: Bhavna, on the phone, said, "Stop talking to Anjum or we're done. And I want to see your chats." When I asked why, she said I obviously didn't love her enough. It's the third time this month she's said "do this or I leave", and each time the list gets longer. I noticed my hands were cold, and I felt scared to text Anjum back.
That's the difference, I think. Mohan's is a boundary about his own room. Bhavna's is about controlling who I talk to. I called Didi at ten. She listened, and said I can stay at hers this weekend while I work it out.
Vikas

qa.q: Why did Mohan give his ultimatum?
qa.a: The smoke gets into his room and he can't breathe properly.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel after Bhavna's call?
qa.a: Vikas felt scared and uneasy, with cold hands and fear of texting Anjum back, sensing control rather than a fair request.

qa.q: What did Vikas do after noticing the difference?
qa.a: Wrote both ultimatums down to think clearly and called Didi the same night, who offered a place to stay that weekend.

qa.q: How does Mohan's ultimatum look from Mohan's side?
qa.a: As a necessary boundary to protect his health in his own room, leaving Vikas a fair choice.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult telling apart an ultimatum that states a real boundary from one that pressures and controls, and seeking support when fear appears.

subtype: Appeals to emotion, authority and logic [Interpreting]
passage:
At the career fair, a man in a blazer had just finished his pitch, and Eshaan was already reaching for the form.
"Farida, did you hear him? Only ten seats left, and a famous professor designed the course. I should sign up now."
"Wait. Let's split what he actually said. Ten seats, decide today: that's urgency."
"Okay, but the professor?"
"That's authority. Could be real. Did he say which professor, or what the course covers?"
"...No. He said I look like someone who'll go far."
"And that's flattery. Nice, but it isn't evidence."
"So it's all a trick?"
"Not all. The bit about past students' placements was an argument, and he had a printed list. That's the part to check. And feeling excited isn't wrong. I felt it too."
"So what do I do?"
"Take the brochure, ask for the list, look up the professor tonight. If the seats vanish by tomorrow, they vanish."
Eshaan slowly put the pen down. "My heart's racing and nothing's even happened."

qa.q: How many seats did the man say were left?
qa.a: Ten.

qa.q: Why was Farida wary of the pitch?
qa.a: Farida felt cautious and suspicious of the urgency and flattery, while honestly admitting to feeling excited too.

qa.q: What does Farida suggest instead of signing on the spot?
qa.a: Take the brochure, ask for the placement list, look up the professor that night, and accept that seats may vanish.

qa.q: What was the pitch like for Eshaan?
qa.a: It left Eshaan excited and rushed, heart racing, ready to sign before knowing what the course covered.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult picking out appeals to urgency, authority, flattery and evidence in a sales pitch and weighing the evidence before acting.

subtype: Negotiating shared living or study arrangements [Expressing]
passage: The kitchen of the flat in Lisbon had become a battlefield of unwashed pans. Tomas finally put the kettle on and sat down across from Yuki. "Can we sort this out properly?" Yuki folded her arms. "I cook every night. You never clean." Tomas took a breath. "Okay. What matters most to you?" She thought. "Coming home to a clean kitchen. I'm exhausted after the late shift at the lab." "For me it's mornings," he said. "I start work at six, so I can't do dishes late at night." They looked at each other. The problem wasn't who was lazy. Yuki suggested it: she'd cook and leave the pans to soak; he'd wash everything at six, before leaving. Bins and bathroom they'd alternate weekly, and the electricity bill they'd split in half. Tomas wrote it on a sheet of paper, they both signed it with mock ceremony, and taped it to the fridge. Three weeks later the paper was splashed with sauce, but the kitchen was clean.

qa.q: What time does Tomas start work?
qa.a: At six.

qa.q: Why did Tomas ask what mattered most instead of defending himself?
qa.a: Tomas was probably stung by "you never clean" but stayed calm, wanting to solve the problem rather than win the argument.

qa.q: What made the negotiation work?
qa.a: Each named what mattered to them instead of blaming, they built an option that fit both schedules, and they wrote the deal down on the fridge.

qa.q: What was the dirty kitchen like for Yuki?
qa.a: Exhausting and frustrating after late lab shifts, which is why a clean kitchen mattered most to her.

grounding: It illustrates young adults negotiating chores by stating interests rather than positions, finding an option that serves both, and writing it down.

qa.q: What did Yamini's Nani run in Lucknow?

qa.q: How did Indu feel when Yamini asked about Indu's parents?

qa.q: What made Yamini's response to Indu's "not yet" a good one?

grounding: It illustrates a young adult sharing family stories to be known while choosing to keep some private details until ready, and a friend respecting that choice.

passage:
Deepika: saw the news about flooding near your hostel!! are you okay??
Dolma: bit of a damp week tbh
Dolma: my ground floor room is now more of an indoor pond. my chappals have gone on a journey
Deepika: DOLMA. how deep is it
Dolma: knee-high at the worst. we're all upstairs in the common room now, the warden brought khichdi
Dolma: mild inconvenience. would give it two stars
Deepika: 😅 okay I'm laughing but also, are you actually okay
Dolma: honestly? lost my notes and my laptop charger and I'm a bit shaken
Dolma: but safe. and dry-ish
Deepika: I'm sending you a charger today. and call me tonight
Dolma: you're a good friend. five stars 🙂

qa.q: What did the warden bring?
qa.a: Khichdi.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling behind the jokes?
qa.a: Dolma was shaken after losing notes and a charger, using understatement to cope while being safe.

qa.q: What was wise about Deepika's reply?
qa.a: Deepika laughed along but also asked directly whether Dolma was actually okay, then offered practical help and a call.

qa.q: How might someone who didn't know about the flood read "bit of a damp week"?
qa.a: As a small complaint about the weather, missing the irony, since understatement only works when the true scale is shared.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult using dry understatement to cope after a flood, and how it depends on shared understanding of the true scale.
